methods.label: Count how often each multiple of seven appears
methods.explanation:
Expanding \(51^!=1!\cdot2!\cdots51!\) repeats many integer factors. We can count the factors of \(7\) by tracking those repeated integers instead of calculating the enormous product.

For example, the integer \(7\) appears once in every factorial from \(7!\) through \(51!\). That is
\[
51-7+1=45
\]
appearances. More generally, an integer \(k\) appears once in each factorial from \(k!\) through \(51!\), for \(52-k\) appearances.

Only multiples of \(7\) contribute factors of \(7\). The multiples at most \(51\), with their numbers of appearances, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
7&:\ 45, &14&:\ 38,\\
21&:\ 31, &28&:\ 24,\\
35&:\ 17, &42&:\ 10,\\
49&:\ 3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each occurrence of the first six multiples contributes exactly one factor of \(7\). Each occurrence of \(49=7^2\) contributes two. There are no other multiples of \(7\) at most \(51\), so these contributions include every factor of \(7\) in the expanded product, with its correct multiplicity.

The total number is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(45+38+31)+(24+17+10)+2\cdot3\\
&\qquad=114+51+6=\boxed{171}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice \(\text{E}\).
methods.levelReason: Counts repeated multiples directly and explains the extra factor from 49. It requires no general valuation formula, floor notation, or advanced number theory.
